messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elias Vance had always trusted his training and the men who shared his hangar. That certainty fractured during a layover in Germany, when a senior officer he had flown alongside for years turned his quiet hospitality into something calculated and violating. Elias could still feel the suffocating shift in the room, the way the familiar routine of the base suddenly curdled into something entirely unpredictable, and the deliberate dismantling of the respect he had placed in the man’s hands. The betrayal was not merely a single moment; it rewired how he read the world. He began to interpret every glance and hesitation around him as a precursor to danger, his mind clinging to the terrifying certainty that he had been fundamentally deceived by someone he had relied on. This conviction did not stay abstract. The more he judged himself as broken, as a lousy coper who could not even protect his own boundaries, the more his eyes began to hunt for signs of duplicity in every crowded terminal and briefing room. When colleagues paused mid-sentence or changed their routes without explanation, Elias’s breath would catch, his shoulders hiking toward his ears, convinced he was walking into another ambush. Back in the Nevada desert, the cockpit that once demanded his absolute focus now amplified his distress. Sudden schedule scrambles no longer read as standard operational tempo; they felt like the ground giving way beneath his boots. He had come to believe he had lost all faith in the structures meant to keep him safe, both on the ground and in the air. This erosion of trust directly fed his physiology. Every time he braced for the next blow, his heart hammered against his ribs, his body primed and ready to react before a threat even materialized. He would jump at the mundane click of a radio or the heavy tread of a ground crewman walking behind his chair. He spent hours after shift lying in bed, his head tilted toward the hallway, listening for the faintest scrape of a door handle or the whisper of footsteps that might mean someone was entering his apartment. He felt perpetually on guard, even within his own walls, as if the enemy had learned his address. His body’s relentless readiness slowly poisoned his daily routine. The constant startle responses made him miss critical briefings, and his need to verify every exit in a room drew sharp looks from his flight surgeon. Over the months, these reactions did not fade; they hardened into a quiet desperation. He was certain that his own reactions since the event proved he was fundamentally failing, and that the world outside his airman’s quarters offered no genuine sanctuary. The tighter his chest constricted, the more his body flinched at ordinary shifts in routine, and the more he expected unpredictability to strike from any blind corner. He had tried to push through the drills, but the physical toll and the emotional isolation had become unsustainable. What finally brought him to the clinic was the morning he realized he could no longer look at his co-pilot without bracing for a violation, and that his own hands would tremble too badly to keep the jet level. He was seeking a way to quiet the constant alarm in his chest, hoping to find a place where he could finally lower his guard without feeling like he was walking into another trap.
